faq.a: Early-stage fibrosis can regress with removal of the cause and effective antiviral or lifestyle therapy.
APRI uses routine labs, requires no equipment, and provides reasonable accuracy for ruling out advanced fibrosis.
faq.q: Why use APRI instead of FibroScan in low‑resource hospitals?

faq.a: Arrange ultrasound for portal hypertension signs and refer for endoscopy to screen varices.
faq.q: What is the next step if APRI suggests cirrhosis but FibroScan is unavailable?

ai.title: Liver Fibrosis Assessment
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Assessing liver fibrosis combines history, exam, and targeted investigations to stage chronic liver disease, guide management, and predict outcomes, especially where resources are limited.

b: Fibrosis is reversible early; later stages become irreversible.
Common in hepatitis B/C, alcohol, NAFLD, schistosomiasis, HIV‑TB co‑infection.
sections.p: Liver fibrosis is the accumulation of scar tissue after chronic injury. It progresses from mild fibrosis to cirrhosis, impairing hepatic function and increasing portal hypertension risk.

b: APRI and FIB‑4 use routine labs.
Clinical signs of portal hypertension appear late.
sections.p: Fibrosis is graded by histologic or non‑invasive scores. In low‑resource settings, simple scores and bedside signs are essential.

b: F4: screen for varices, HCC, and decompensation.
sections.p: Staging determines need for antiviral therapy, surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma, and timing of referral for specialist care or transplant.

t.b: Is there disproportionate AST elevation suggesting advanced fibrosis? Ratio >1 supports F≥2.
Low platelets (<150 ×10⁹/L) indicate portal hypertension and higher fibrosis stage.
Answers: Is fibrosis likely? APRI >1.0 suggests F≥2; >2.0 suggests cirrhosis.
Answers: What is the fibrosis stage? FIB‑4 >3.25 indicates advanced fibrosis; ≤1.45 suggests minimal fibrosis.
Answers: What is liver stiffness? >9.5 kPa = F≥2; >12.5 kPa = cirrhosis. If unavailable, rely on APRI/FIB‑4.
Answers: Are there morphological signs of fibrosis? Coarse echotexture, nodularity, splenomegaly, collateral vessels.
Answers: What is the exact histologic stage? Gold standard; use METAVIR. Reserve for unclear cases.

b: Antiviral therapy for HBV/HCV reduces fibrosis progression.
Alcohol cessation, weight loss for NAFLD, anti‑schistosomal praziquantel.
Vaccinate against hepatitis A/B, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, monitor progression, and manage complications.

b: Fatty liver (steatosis) may raise ALT but does not cause fibrosis alone.
Acute hepatitis can raise AST/ALT dramatically without fibrosis.
sections.p: Cirrhosis vs. advanced fibrosis; both show portal hypertension but cirrhosis has architectural nodularity and irreversible scarring.

b: APRI may underestimate fibrosis in patients with thrombocytopenia from other causes.
FIB‑4 uses age; older patients may appear more fibrotic.
sections.p: Transient elastography can be falsely high in acute inflammation or cholestasis; low platelet counts may be due to HIV or malaria, not only fibrosis.

b: FIB‑4 uses age, AST, ALT, platelet; easy to calculate on paper.
sections.p: Focus on clinical reasoning: combine bedside signs with simple scores; know when to refer for elastography or biopsy.

b: Assuming normal ALT rules out fibrosis.
Skipping variceal screening in patients with F4.
sections.p: Relying on a single test, ignoring local disease patterns, or delaying referral for decompensation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with hypotension (possible ruptured variceal bleed).
New onset encephalopathy or jaundice in known fibrosis (decompensation).
